triage.name: Tooth Decay
triage.reason: Patients present with dental pain or sensitivity; diagnosis is reachable by history and exam, though definitive management is dental rather than medical.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'periapical dental radiograph' was in ['initial', 'confirmatory'], kept ['initial']
presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

age.peak: bimodal: children and adolescents, and older adults

demographics: One of the most common chronic conditions worldwide, affecting people of all ages
Higher prevalence in children and adolescents, and again in older adults with receding gums and exposed root surfaces
More common in lower-income and rural populations with less access to dental care and fluoridated water

risk_factors.text: Poor oral hygiene (infrequent brushing or flossing)
Frequent intake of sugary or starchy foods and drinks, especially between meals
Inadequate fluoride exposure (no fluoridated water or fluoride toothpaste)
Dry mouth from medications, disease, or cancer treatment
Bottle feeding with juice or at bedtime in infants and toddlers
Receding gums and exposed root surfaces in older adults
Crowded or deeply grooved teeth that are hard to clean

family_history: Dental caries in a parent or sibling
social_history: Limited access to dental care or no regular dental check-ups
Living in an area without community water fluoridation
Frequent snacking or sipping sugary drinks throughout the day
exposures: Medications or conditions that reduce saliva

chief_complaints.text: My tooth is sensitive to sweets, hot, or cold
I see a dark spot or hole in my tooth
My gums or face are swollen and it hurts

hpi.onset: Gradual; early decay causes no symptoms, and pain or sensitivity appears only as the decay progresses
hpi.duration: Weeks to months of intermittent sensitivity before pain becomes persistent; an abscess can develop over days
hpi.progression: Starts as a white or brown spot on the tooth surface with no symptoms, then causes sensitivity to sweets, hot, or cold, then a constant toothache, and finally infection with an abscess, facial swelling, and fever if untreated
hpi.location: A single tooth or a few teeth, most often the chewing surfaces of back teeth or between teeth; older adults may have decay at the gum line
hpi.radiation: Pain may radiate to the ear, jaw, or side of the face when the pulp is involved
hpi.quality: Sharp and brief with hot, cold, or sweet foods early on; later a dull, throbbing, constant ache
hpi.severity: Mild and intermittent early; moderate to severe and constant once the pulp is involved
hpi.timing: Initially only with eating or drinking; later constant and worse at night
relieving: Avoiding the trigger foods and drinks
Over-the-counter pain relievers such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen

associated_symptoms.text: Tooth sensitivity to sweets, hot, or cold
Visible white or brown spot or hole in the tooth
Bad breath or a bad taste in the mouth
Food getting stuck in the tooth

pertinent_negatives: Difficulty swallowing or opening the mouth
Severe pain that wakes the patient from sleep
Pain that started suddenly after a dental procedure
History of head and neck radiation

argues_against: Fever with facial swelling suggests spread of infection beyond the tooth

positives.text: Pain radiating to the ear or jaw

argues_against: Difficulty swallowing or trismus suggests a deep neck space infection rather than simple caries
Frequent vomiting or reflux suggests dental erosion rather than decay
Facial swelling with fever suggests an abscess or cellulitis

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not report pain and instead show irritability, poor feeding, or refusal to chew; decay in baby teeth can progress quickly.
Decay often occurs on exposed root surfaces at the gum line and may cause little pain because of receding gums and reduced pulp sensitivity.
missing_classic_features: Visible cavity on the chewing surface

atypical.how_it_differs: Changes in saliva, diet, and oral hygiene can increase decay; nausea and vomiting may cause erosion, and dental care is often delayed.
Decay can progress faster and infection can spread more readily, with less obvious pain or swelling.

general.moderate: Mild discomfort when speaking or chewing, otherwise well-appearing
general.severe: Uncomfortable, holds the jaw or cheek, avoids chewing on the affected side
general.critical: Ill-appearing, febrile, with facial swelling or drooling, reluctant to open the mouth

findings.maneuver: Inspect the teeth with a light and tongue blade, examining all surfaces including between teeth and along the gum line
findings.finding: A dark brown or black hole or pit in the tooth surface

findings.maneuver: Inspect the teeth after drying the surface with gauze
findings.finding: A chalky white spot on the enamel, indicating early mineral loss
Brown discoloration or staining of the tooth

findings.maneuver: Gently probe the suspicious tooth surface with a dental explorer or tongue blade
findings.finding: The probe catches or sticks in a softened, cavitated area, and the patient reports tenderness

findings.maneuver: Tap the affected tooth lightly with the handle of a dental mirror or a tongue blade
findings.finding: Pain on percussion, suggesting involvement of the pulp or periapical tissues

findings.maneuver: Apply a cold stimulus (ice or cold spray) to the affected tooth and compare with an adjacent normal tooth
findings.finding: Sharp, brief pain that resolves quickly after the stimulus is removed

findings.maneuver: Apply a cold stimulus to the affected tooth
findings.finding: Pain that lingers for more than a few seconds after the stimulus is removed, suggesting irreversible pulpitis

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the face and jaw for asymmetry, swelling, or warmth
findings.finding: Unilateral facial or jaw swelling, warm and tender to palpation

findings.maneuver: Inspect the buccal mucosa and gingiva adjacent to the affected tooth
findings.finding: Localized swelling or a fluctuant, pus-filled swelling (abscess) near the tooth root

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to open the mouth fully and measure the interincisal distance
findings.finding: Limited mouth opening (trismus), suggesting spread of infection to the masticator space

findings.maneuver: Palpate the submandibular and submental areas and the cervical lymph nodes
findings.finding: Tender, enlarged submandibular lymph nodes or diffuse neck tenderness

findings.maneuver: Assess the airway by listening to the voice, observing for drooling, and checking for stridor
findings.finding: Normal voice, no drooling, no stridor, and no difficulty breathing

findings.maneuver: Inspect the teeth and gums for plaque, tartar, and gingival inflammation
findings.finding: Good oral hygiene with minimal plaque and healthy-appearing gums

findings.maneuver: Palpate or percuss the maxillary and frontal sinuses
Palpate the temporomandibular joints and ask the patient to open and close the mouth
findings.finding: No temporomandibular joint tenderness or clicking

labs.caveat: Only rises when decay has progressed to an odontogenic abscess or spreading infection; a normal white count is expected in simple caries.
Nonspecific; supports an inflammatory or infectious complication rather than the caries itself.
Undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes raises caries risk and worsens infection; check when the presentation is severe or recurrent.

imaging.preferred_when: A single tooth is symptomatic and the question is pulp or periapical involvement

findings.text: Radiolucent defect in the enamel and dentin of the affected tooth
Loss of the normal periodontal ligament space or a periapical radiolucency suggesting apical periodontitis or abscess
No periapical lucency (early or superficial decay)

imaging.preferred_when: Routine caries detection and surveillance, especially between teeth and in children

findings.text: Radiolucent lesions in the interproximal enamel or dentin
No cavitated lesions (early or arrested caries)

imaging.preferred_when: Widespread disease, suspected impacted teeth, or when a full-mouth survey is needed

findings.text: Multiple carious lesions across several teeth

imaging.study: CT of the maxillofacial region with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected deep space infection, facial cellulitis, or airway compromise

findings.text: Periosteal reaction or cortical breach at the apex of the offending tooth
Abscess cavity with rim enhancement in the buccal, submandibular, or masticator space
Soft tissue swelling and fat stranding of the face or neck
Airway narrowing or deviation from a deep neck space collection

initial.why: Confirms the depth of the carious lesion and shows periapical involvement in a symptomatic tooth
Detects interproximal caries and screens the other teeth
Looks for leukocytosis when an abscess or spreading infection is suspected
initial.only_if: fever, facial swelling, or systemic symptoms are present

supporting.why: Shows the full dentition when disease is widespread or an impacted tooth is suspected
supporting.only_if: multiple teeth are involved or a full-mouth survey is needed

supporting.why: Supports an inflammatory or infectious complication when the diagnosis is unclear
Identifies diabetes that raises caries risk and worsens infection
supporting.only_if: severe, recurrent, or nonhealing dental disease is present

not_indicated.test: CT of the maxillofacial region with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed for simple caries; reserved for suspected deep space infection or airway compromise
not_indicated.only_if: a deep space infection, facial cellulitis, or airway compromise is suspected

not_indicated.why: Routine chemistry is not needed for uncomplicated dental caries
Nonspecific and adds nothing to the dental examination and radiographs
No role in the evaluation of dental caries or a localized odontogenic abscess
Only useful if sepsis from a spreading odontogenic infection is suspected

decision_points: Dental radiographs are the key test; medical labs are only for suspected systemic infection
Facial swelling, trismus, drooling, or difficulty swallowing requires urgent CT and dental or surgical drainage
Pregnancy: dental radiographs are safe with shielding; defer only nonurgent imaging

differential.name: Pulpitis (reversible or irreversible)
differential.why_considered: Dental pain and sensitivity to hot or cold are the hallmark of both caries and pulp inflammation

history: Pain triggered by thermal stimuli; in irreversible pulpitis the pain lingers after the stimulus is removed and may wake the patient at night
No visible hole or only a deep restoration may be present
exam: A deep carious lesion or restoration may be seen, but the pulp is the source of pain
Percussion may be tender if the periapical tissues are involved
imaging: Deep caries approaching or involving the pulp on periapical radiograph
No periapical radiolucency in reversible pulpitis; may be present in irreversible pulpitis

differential.name: Periapical abscess
differential.why_considered: A toothache that becomes constant and severe with swelling suggests infection extending beyond the tooth
differential.trigger: Facial or gum swelling, fever, or severe constant pain

history: Constant, throbbing pain that may be relieved by cold in early abscess but worsens with heat
Swelling of the gum or face, bad taste, fever
exam: Tender, swollen gum or fluctuant swelling near the tooth apex
Facial swelling, tender regional lymph nodes, fever
labs: Leukocytosis and elevated CRP when systemic infection is present
imaging: Periapical radiolucency or widened periodontal ligament space on dental radiograph
CT shows abscess cavity with rim enhancement if deep space involvement is suspected

differential.name: Periodontal disease (gingivitis or periodontitis)
differential.why_considered: Gum inflammation, bleeding, and bad breath can be mistaken for caries-related problems

history: Gums that bleed when brushing, persistent bad breath, loose teeth
Pain is less common than with caries; discomfort is often diffuse
exam: Gingival redness, swelling, and bleeding on probing
Periodontal pockets, gum recession, and tooth mobility
imaging: Alveolar bone loss on dental radiographs
No cavitated carious lesion in the symptomatic area

differential.name: Dental erosion
differential.why_considered: Loss of tooth structure from acid can cause sensitivity and visible changes that resemble decay

history: Frequent vomiting, reflux, or high intake of acidic foods and drinks
Sensitivity is often widespread rather than localized to one tooth
exam: Smooth, glossy, or cupped-out tooth surfaces, often on the palatal surfaces of upper front teeth
No soft, catchable cavity on probing
imaging: Generalized loss of enamel thickness without a localized radiolucent defect

differential.name: Sinusitis
differential.why_considered: Maxillary sinus pain can radiate to the upper teeth and mimic a toothache

history: Recent upper respiratory infection, nasal congestion, facial pressure
Pain is worse when bending forward; multiple upper teeth may ache
exam: Tenderness over the maxillary sinuses, purulent nasal discharge
Teeth appear normal on inspection and probing
imaging: Sinus opacification or air-fluid level on CT or plain radiograph
No carious lesion on dental radiographs

differential.name: Trigeminal neuralgia
differential.why_considered: Sharp, electric shock-like facial pain can be mistaken for dental pain

history: Brief, lancinating pain triggered by touch, chewing, or cold air
Pain follows a trigeminal distribution and is not provoked by sweet foods
exam: Teeth and gums are normal; no cavity or tenderness on probing
Neurologic exam may show a trigger zone
imaging: Dental radiographs are normal; MRI may show neurovascular compression

differential.name: Temporomandibular disorder
differential.why_considered: Jaw pain and pain with chewing can be attributed to a tooth

history: Jaw clicking, locking, or pain that is worse with chewing and in the morning
Pain is often diffuse and not triggered by sweets or temperature
exam: Tenderness of the masticatory muscles or temporomandibular joint, limited or asymmetric opening
Teeth are normal on inspection and probing
imaging: Dental radiographs are normal; MRI or CT may show joint changes

severity.mild: Early, non-cavitated decay: a white spot or shallow enamel lesion with no or only mild sensitivity to sweets or cold; no pain at rest
severity.moderate: Cavitated decay limited to enamel or outer dentin: a visible hole, sensitivity to hot, cold, or sweets, and mild discomfort with chewing
severity.severe: Deep decay involving the pulp: constant toothache, lingering pain after hot or cold, pain on percussion, and possible early periapical infection without systemic signs
severity.critical: Odontogenic infection with facial or neck swelling, fever, trismus, drooling, or difficulty swallowing, suggesting a deep space infection or airway compromise

red_flags.finding: Facial or neck swelling with fever
red_flags.meaning: Spread of infection beyond the tooth; needs urgent dental or surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Trismus or difficulty opening the mouth
red_flags.meaning: Infection involving the masticator space; risk of deep neck space spread

red_flags.finding: Drooling, difficulty swallowing, or voice change
red_flags.meaning: Possible airway compromise from a deep space infection; emergency

red_flags.finding: Severe pain that wakes the patient from sleep or is not relieved by over-the-counter analgesics
red_flags.meaning: Irreversible pulpitis or periapical infection requiring prompt dental care

complications.name: Pulpitis and periapical abscess
clues: Lingering pain after hot or cold

complications.name: Facial cellulitis or deep space infection
clues: CT showing abscess in buccal, submandibular, or masticator space

special_populations.differences: Young children may not report pain and instead show irritability, poor feeding, or refusal to chew; decay in baby teeth can progress quickly and affect permanent teeth.
Decay often occurs on exposed root surfaces at the gum line and may cause little pain because of receding gums and reduced pulp sensitivity; more likely to have dry mouth from medications.
Changes in saliva, diet, and oral hygiene can increase decay; nausea and vomiting may cause erosion, and dental care is often delayed. Dental radiographs are safe with shielding.
Decay can progress faster and infection can spread more readily, with less obvious pain or swelling; a lower threshold for imaging and antibiotics is warranted.
Poorly controlled diabetes raises caries risk and worsens infection; check glucose when the presentation is severe or recurrent.

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and can you point to the exact tooth?
key_questions.looking_for: Localized to one tooth or a few teeth, often a back tooth or between teeth

key_questions.question: What brings the pain on?
key_questions.looking_for: Triggered by sweets, hot, or cold foods and drinks; later pain at rest

key_questions.question: Does the pain go away quickly after the trigger is removed, or does it linger?
key_questions.looking_for: Brief pain suggests reversible disease; lingering pain suggests pulp involvement

key_questions.question: How long has this been going on, and is it getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Weeks to months of intermittent sensitivity progressing to constant pain

key_questions.question: Does it hurt when you bite down or chew on that side?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain on biting suggests periapical involvement

key_questions.question: Have you noticed a dark spot, hole, or food getting stuck in the tooth?
key_questions.looking_for: Visible cavity or retained food, supporting cavitated decay

key_questions.question: Is the pain worse at night or when you lie down?
key_questions.looking_for: Nocturnal or positional pain suggests irreversible pulpitis

key_questions.question: Any swelling of the gum, face, or jaw, or any fever?
key_questions.looking_for: Swelling or fever suggests an abscess or spreading infection

key_questions.question: Any trouble opening your mouth, swallowing, or drooling?
key_questions.looking_for: Trismus, dysphagia, or drooling suggests deep space infection or airway risk

key_questions.question: How often do you brush and floss, and do you use fluoride toothpaste?
key_questions.looking_for: Infrequent brushing or flossing and no fluoride exposure

key_questions.question: How often do you eat or drink sugary or starchy things between meals?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequent snacking or sipping sugary drinks throughout the day

key_questions.question: When did you last see a dentist, and do you have access to dental care?
key_questions.looking_for: No regular dental check-ups or limited access to care

key_questions.question: Does your mouth feel dry, and are you taking any medicines that dry it out?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticholinergics, antihistamines, antidepressants, diuretics, or opioids reducing saliva

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, Sjögren syndrome, reflux, or an eating disorder with vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that raise caries risk or cause erosion

key_questions.question: Have you had radiation to the head or neck, or chemotherapy?
key_questions.looking_for: Dry mouth from cancer treatment raising caries risk

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have a lot of cavities?
Do you use tobacco, including smokeless tobacco?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco use raising caries and gum disease risk

key_questions.question: Has there been any recent injury to the tooth or a recent dental procedure?
key_questions.looking_for: Trauma or recent dental work as an alternative cause of pain

reasoning_points: Tooth pain or sensitivity triggered by sweets, hot, or cold, often localized to one tooth
Risk factors such as poor oral hygiene, frequent sugary or starchy intake, and inadequate fluoride
Visible white spot, brown stain, or cavitated hole on the tooth surface
Tenderness or a catch when probing the softened tooth surface
Pain on percussion or lingering pain after cold suggesting pulp or periapical involvement
Dental radiograph showing a radiolucent defect in enamel or dentin, with periapical changes if the pulp is involved
No facial swelling, fever, trismus, or airway symptoms unless the infection has spread
Alternative causes such as pulpitis, periodontal disease, sinusitis, trigeminal neuralgia, or temporomandibular disorder considered and excluded

easy: Young or middle-aged adult with a classic story of sensitivity to sweets and cold in one tooth
Visible dark cavity on a back tooth
Probe catches in a softened area and the patient winces
No fever, swelling, or systemic symptoms
medium: Pain that lingers after cold or wakes the patient at night, suggesting pulp involvement
Decay between teeth with no visible cavity on the chewing surface
Older adult with decay at the gum line on an exposed root surface and little pain
Patient with dry mouth from medications and multiple affected teeth
hard: Young child who cannot localize pain and instead is irritable or refuses to chew
Upper molar pain that turns out to be maxillary sinusitis
Sharp, electric facial pain from trigeminal neuralgia mistaken for a toothache
Jaw pain from temporomandibular disorder with normal teeth
Severe decay presenting with facial swelling, fever, or trismus suggesting a deep space infection
